elements.text:
Case Study 1 - Anna (late teens)

Anna is a 19-year-old woman who has always tried to live up to high expectations - both her own and those of her family and friends. On the outside, Anna seems confident and successful: she excelled at school, earning top grades, and secured a place to study medicine at a good university. Her future looks bright, and everyone around her tells her so. She is well-liked by her peers, and stays involved in her church - she is an active member of the church band, and also helps to organise teens events. To others, she seems to be thriving - a picture of success, confidence, and balance.

But beneath the surface, Anna is wrestling with inner turmoil. She feels like she’s constantly switching between two extremes. At times, after receiving praise from a teacher or finishing a challenging assignment, she feels proud of her accomplishments and tells herself that she’s on the right track. But these moments don’t last. Other times, especially if anything goes wrong, she feels like a fraud, doubting her abilities and feeling crushed by the fear that she’ll never measure up.

This inner tension is exhausting for Anna. When she looks at others, she either compares herself favourably and feels pride, or she feels inadequate and spirals into insecurity and anxiety. She’s not sure who she really is, and she’s starting to wonder if she will know. Recently, Anna has been praying about her identity, asking God to help her understand herself more clearly. But she still struggles with feelings of confusion, not knowing how to reconcile her strengths and weaknesses. She has also begun avoiding deep conversations with her family and friends, fearful that if she opens up about her struggles, they’ll be disappointed in her or see her as weak.

Anna wonders: ‘How do I truly understand myself? Will I ever find peace, or will I always be torn between extremes?’ She longs for clarity, but she feels trapped in a cycle of confusion, pride, self-doubt, and anxiety.

“We are not very good at recognizing illusions, least of all the ones we cherish about ourselves - the ones we are born with and which feed the roots of sin.”
Thomas Merton

“The more we try to understand ourselves, the more lost we get. True freedom is not in figuring out who we are, but in forgetting ourselves and looking to Christ.”
Tim Keller

“Man is neither angel nor beast, and unhappily whoever wants to act the angel, acts the beast.”
Blaise Pascal

“We do not know ourselves until we have learned to look at ourselves from God’s perspective. We are strangers to our own hearts.”
C.S. Lewis

elements.text:
Case Study 1b - Anna shaped by truth

The enigma of the heart - including its deceitfulness - explains why it is so hard for Anna to see herself clearly. When she compares herself to others, her heart tricks her into either feeling prideful or insecure, depending on whom she’s comparing herself to. But Anna’s identity cannot be found by measuring herself against others. As she learns to step away from these comparisons, she will begin to see herself more clearly - not through the lens of human standards, but through God’s eyes.

Anna’s turning point will come when she realizes that true self-understanding comes from knowing God. It is as we ask God to search our hearts and reveal the truth that we can begin to understand who we really are. Anna needs to stop relying on her own assessment and start relying on God’s view of her.

God created Anna and knows her intimately. He sees both her strengths and her weaknesses and loves her deeply, not because of what she has achieved but because she is His child. By focusing on who God is and how He sees her, Anna can find the peace she has been searching for. She doesn’t need to live in the tension between pride and insecurity - she can rest in the knowledge that her identity is secure in Christ.

As Anna learns to look to Christ for her identity, she will begin to understand herself in a new way. Instead of fixating on her achievements or failures, she can focus on Christ’s love, grace, and sacrifice.

Anna’s feelings of confusion and frustration are normal for a believer, but they don’t define her. By turning to Christ, she can find the strength to overcome the battle within herself and live in the freedom that comes from being made new in Him.

For Anna, the path forward involves regularly seeking God’s perspective on her life. Replacing her thoughts of pride or insecurity with biblical truth will help her see herself more clearly. She can spend time asking God to reveal any areas where her view of herself is distorted. Anna can invite trusted friends or mentors to speak truth into her life, helping her discern areas where she may be blind to her strengths or weaknesses.

Case Study 2 - Mark (late-20s)

Mark is a 29-year-old software engineer who has always been a high achiever. He began his career straight out of college, landing a good job at a fast-growing tech company. Over the years, he worked long hours, tackled difficult projects, and consistently delivered results. His dedication paid off as he quickly climbed the ranks, earning praise from his supervisors and becoming known as the go-to person for complex problems.

But as time has gone by, Mark’s sense of self-worth began to shift. He always took pride in his skills and achievements, but recently he has started to depend more and more on his performance at work. Every successful project makes him feel validated and important. But if he fails at a project - or even if he succeeds, but his contributions aren’t particularly recognised or celebrated - he feels like a failure, and starts to doubt himself.

Recently, Mark experienced a major setback. He had been eyeing a promotion that he believed he was more than qualified for. He had worked tirelessly for months, hoping his efforts would secure him the promotion. But when the announcement came, the position was given to someone else - a colleague whom Mark considered less capable and less hard-working. The news shook him to his core. He felt frustrated, undervalued and also deeply insecure. He began to question whether he was as good as he thought and whether his hard work had even been worth it.

Mark also struggles with seeing the value in others, especially those he thinks are less talented, or less successful, or less driven. He finds himself becoming critical of coworkers who don’t put in the same effort he does, and he has a hard time showing kindness to people who seem to ’get in the way’ of his progress. In his quieter moments, Mark realises he’s measuring himself and others by the wrong standards, but he’s not sure how to stop.

Mark asks himself: ‘If I’m not successful or recognized for my hard work, what’s my real worth?’ He also wonders how can he learn to see value in others when they seem to fall so short so often.

You created us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless
until they rest in You.
Augustine

Man is neither angel nor beast
Blaise Pascal

People travel to wonder at the height of the mountains, at the huge waves of the seas, at the long course of the rivers, at the vast compass of the ocean, at the circular motion of the stars, and yet they pass by the mystery of themselves without wondering.

elements.text: The image of God is not shared by any animal, nor anything else in all creation, not even the angels. Humanity is the image of God (1 Corinthians 11:7). The emphasis falls not on one aspect of our constitution (e.g. rationality, or spirituality) but on who we are, and the situation in which God has put us, and the role he has given us. We are defined in relationship to God. We are the created representation of the Creator; we are the concrete manifestation of his glory here on earth.

elements.text: When God announces his intention to create humanity, He says ’Let us make’ - which suggests plurality and relationship within God Himself. Relationship is built on the plurality of, and distinction between, people. Relationship is fundamental to who God is, and now it is being made fundamental to who human beings are. Relationship is built into us from the very moment of our creation - indeed, from the very moment of our conception in the mind of God. Relationships are not an accidental extra, added to creation as an afterthought. They are at the heart of reality, at the centre of who God is, and core to who humans are.

elements.text:
Case Study 2b - Mark and the image of God

Mark’s struggle with his self-worth stems from a misunderstanding of where his value truly lies. He has been measuring his worth based on his performance and success at work. But our worth comes from the fact that we are created in the image of God. This means that Mark’s value is not dependent on his achievements - it is inherent in who he already is, because God made him. He doesn’t need to earn his worth - it was given to him by his Creator. By understanding this, Mark can begin to let go of the pressure to constantly prove himself and find peace in the knowledge that he is already valuable in God’s eyes.

Mark will also find it easier to see value in others if he can fully take on board the truth that we are all made in the image of God. Every person, regardless of their achievements or failures, is made in God’s likeness. For Mark, this means that even those coworkers he finds frustrating or less capable are still worthy of respect and love because they, too, bear God’s image. If Mark can start to see others as God sees them, he will be able to show more grace, kindness, and understanding. Instead of measuring people by this world’s standards of success, he can learn to value them as God’s creations, just as he values himself.

Being made in the image of God means being dependent on Him. We are not self-sufficient - we are derivative, reflecting God’s glory. Mark’s desire for recognition and success may well stem from a desire to be self-sufficient, to prove his worth without relying on anyone else - not even God. But God created us to do great things as we depend on Him. He didn’t create us to strive for independence. If Mark can accept his dependency on God’s grace and provision, he will find freedom from the constant pressure to perform. Instead of trying to prove himself through his work, Mark can focus on reflecting God’s character in how he treats others, finding purpose in that reflection rather than in recognition by the world.

We were created for community. Mark’s drive for success has led him to isolate himself from others, viewing them as competition rather than companions. But recognising that relationships are central to being made in God’s image will help Mark build healthier connections with those around him. By valuing relationships and teamwork, Mark can begin to foster a community that reflects God’s love and unity. This shift in perspective will not only enrich Mark’s own life but also benefit those he works with, as he starts to see them as partners rather than obstacles.

Case Study 3 - Sarah (late-30s)

Sarah is a 37-year-old Christian who loves God and has been following Christ faithfully for years. She is active in her church, leads a small group, and often encourages others in their faith. From the outside she shows many signs of spiritual maturity - she is someone others look up to for guidance and wisdom. But despite this, internally Sarah struggles deeply with feelings of guilt and shame over her past mistakes. She constantly feels as though she’s not good enough for God’s love. She knows, intellectually, that she’s forgiven through Christ. But so often in practice she finds herself feeling like her sins and mistakes define her.

Sarah often finds herself caught in a cycle of sin and repentance. She confesses her sins, feels forgiven for a short time, but soon after falls back into old habits of anger, jealousy, and impatience. Each time she stumbles, the weight of guilt grows heavier, and she starts to believe that God must be fed up with her. Sarah is afraid that she’ll never escape this cycle and wonders if she’s truly changed at all.

She was listening to a sermon once, and the preacher got people to imagine that God had appeared to them visibly, and that He was looking at them. The preacher then asked, ‘What expression would you expect to see on God’s face? What expression would be in his eyes as he looks at you?’

As soon as Sarah heard the question, she knew what expression she would see in God’s eyes: disappointment. She could almost picture the look of disapproval she believed God would have as He saw her struggles and shortcomings. It was the expression of someone who had given countless chances, only to be let down again and again.

This moment lingered in Sarah’s mind long after the sermon ended. Since then, she has started asking herself these questions: ‘If I’m really forgiven, why do I still feel so guilty? Why does sin still have such a strong grip on me, even though I’ve been a Christian for so long?’

She doesn’t have an answer.

As the salt flavours every drop in the Atlantic, so does sin affect every atom of our nature. It is so sadly there, so abundantly there, that if you cannot detect it, you are deceived.
Charles Spurgeon

My sin was this, that I looked for pleasure, beauty, and truth not in Him but in myself and His other creatures, and the search led me instead to pain, confusion, and error.
Augustine

elements.text:
Case Study 3b - Sarah

Sarah’s battle with guilt is an example of how sin distorts our view of ourselves and our relationship with God. Sin creates a separation between us and God, and Sarah feels this separation sharply. That’s why she struggles with guilt even after confessing her sins. But it’s important for her to understand that this feeling of separation is not permanent. Sarah needs to recognise that sin affects every part of her being - her thoughts, emotions, and actions. But this awareness is not meant to drive her into despair; it’s meant to lead her to a deeper reliance on God’s grace.

The cycle of sin and guilt that Sarah experiences is part of the ongoing spiritual battle that every believer faces. But Sarah’s ongoing struggle with sin doesn’t negate the work of Christ - it highlights the very reason she needs Him. Sarah’s guilt deceives her into believing her sin is greater than God’s grace. That is not true. God’s grace is more powerful than her sin. When she repents, she is not trying to earn God’s favour - she is responding to the forgiveness that Christ has already provided on the cross. Sarah needs to hold on to this truth: God is transforming her, even in the midst of her struggles. Walking in the light of Christ means trusting His forgiveness and walking in truth, not in guilt. Sarah’s difficulty in accepting that she is forgiven reflects the deeper impact of sin on our relationship with ourselves. Sin causes us to believe lies about our worth and identity, convincing us that we are beyond hope. But as Sarah learns to embrace the truth of God’s grace, she will begin to see herself as God sees her - not with eyes of disappointment, but as eyes of delight. He sees her as his beloved child, forgiven and made new.

Sarah’s feelings of guilt do not define her. Her identity is found in Christ’s victory over sin. As she continues to seek God’s strength and rely on His grace, Sarah will see transformation in her life. She won’t experience immediate freedom from every sinful habit, but she can trust that God is at work within her, shaping her into the image of Christ. Each time she repents and returns to God, she is participating in the process of sanctification. Her battle is not in vain - it is part of the journey toward greater Christlikeness.

Sarah doesn’t need to remain trapped in the cycle of guilt and shame. If she embraces God’s grace, she can find freedom from the weight of sin, because it is already forgiven in Christ. This is the hope that she, and every believer, can hold onto as we navigate the tension between our fallen nature and our identity in Christ.

Case Study 4 - Michael (late 30s)

Michael is a Christian who has been active in his church for many years. He loves God, attends worship regularly, and serves on the church’s leadership team. But in the past few years, his career has begun to demand more and more of his time and attention. Michael is a manager at a growing tech company. He is good at his job, successful and ambitious, and he’s recently been offered a promotion that would increase his income and influence in the industry.

But Michael’s work has already taken a toll on his personal life. His wife, Rachel, has mentioned how much she misses spending time with him, and his children have become used to seeing him only briefly in the mornings before he rushes off to work. They are often in bed before he gets home. Michael’s involvement in church has also started to come under pressure - he’s often too tired or busy to attend Bible studies, he sometimes has to travel with work at weekends, and his prayer life has become more irregular.

Michael loves his family, and wants to see them do well in life. When Rachel has raised the issue of missing him, he has explained that all his hard work is for them, and for their progress. He believes that his career is part of God’s calling on his life. But he is beginning to feel that something is out of balance. Rachel recently confronted him more directly, saying, ‘I know you say you love us, but your actions are telling a different story. We don’t feel like we’re a priority any more.’

Michael is not sure what to do. He wonders: Can you love your family and God while also pursuing success at work? What does it mean to have a ’good balance’ when the demands of life pull you in many directions?

elements.text:
Case Study 4b - Michael & well-ordered love

Michael’s problem is not that he loves his job, nor that he wants to succeed. Work is a good gift from God, and we are called to work diligently. But his love for work is overshadowing his love for God and his family. Michael’s dedication to his job has distanced him from his family and his God. He is not consciously rebelling against God, but he is being drawn toward worldly success as his source of fulfilment.

Michael’s relationships are beginning to suffer. Rachel feels neglected, and his children are missing time with their dad. He may be telling himself he’s providing for his family, but the truth is that his presence and emotional support are more valuable to them than any material comforts his job may provide. Also, Michael’s spiritual life is starting to wither. His relationship with God is becoming secondary to his career ambitions. Michael may not realise it yet, but his disordered love for his work is pulling him away from the true source of joy and peace: God Himself. His misplaced love causes the weariness and frustration that Michael feels at home. His heart, designed to love God first and foremost, is being pulled in the wrong direction. No matter how much success he achieves, it will never satisfy the deeper longing in his soul for a relationship with God and a well-ordered life.

What does Michael need to do to realign his love? It is not (necessarily) about giving up his career or ambitions, but about restoring the proper order of love in his heart. (Although the further the ’disease’ is allowed to grow, the more drastic the ’treatment’ may need to be.) The greatest commandment is to love God with all our heart, soul, mind, and strength. Only when God is at the centre of our love can we rightly love everything else - including our families and our work.

For Michael, this may begin with repentance and prayer: acknowledging that success has drawn his heart away, and so he has neglected his primary love for God. He could also have an honest conversation with his boss about clearer work-life boundaries: perhaps limiting his hours to ensure he’s home in time for dinner, or turning off his phone during family time to be fully present. He should spend quality time with Rachel and his children. This could be as simple as family devotions, or planning regular family activities. He might also include Rachel in discussions about his career ambitions, ensuring that they are of the same mind on what is best for their family. This might mean reconsidering the promotion, if it will cause further damage, or finding ways to balance his professional growth with his family life.

Case Study 5 - Rachel (late 20s)

Rachel is a dedicated Christian. She has served in her local church since her teens. She leads a women’s Bible study, helps with the teens’ fellowship, volunteers in the church’s outreach programs. She’s known for being dependable, generous, and always willing to lend a helping hand. Rachel’s life is full, not only with church responsibilities but she also takes care of her widowed mother, who is not in good health. Rachel also has a full-time job as a high school teacher, which allows her to provide financially for herself and her mother.

For the past year or two, Rachel has felt her energy levels dropping. She is still committed to her faith in Jesus, and she regularly prays and reads her Bible, but she often feels worn out. She knows God is good and finds moments of encouragement in His presence, but the ongoing challenges of life are leaving her emotionally and physically drained. Some days she struggles to find joy even in the activities she used to love, like leading Bible studies and helping at church events. Rachel finds herself asking, ‘Why does life feel so hard, even when I’m trying to follow God faithfully?’ Her prayers for strength seem to be answered with more challenges.

Even with her weariness, Rachel still finds peace and contentment in God. She knows He is with her and there are still moments when she feels His presence encouraging her, but those moments are often fleeting. But the frustrations of her daily life - like difficult students at school, her mother’s health challenges, and conflicts in the church - are taking their toll. These problems pile up, and she sees no end to them. She wonders if she’s doing something wrong or if she just has to endure this difficult season indefinitely.

elements.text:
Case Study 5b - Rachel and Flourishing

Rachel’s weariness doesn’t mean she has failed in her faith or that God has abandoned her. Rather, it reflects the brokenness of this world, where even the most faithful servants experience hardship. Rachel’s contentment in God is a powerful testimony. Just because life is hard doesn’t mean God is not working. In fact, in these difficult moments, God’s sustaining grace often becomes most visible. Rachel can take heart knowing that even when she is weary, God is her refuge and strength. Even though she feels worn down, Rachel is living out the call to love others sacrificially. When she chooses to care for her mother instead of seeking her own comfort, she is reflecting the love of Christ. This is a form of flourishing that the world might not recognize, but it is the kind of flourishing that brings glory to God.

But Rachel also needs to consider how she can flourish physically and practically by addressing the pressures in her life, so she doesn’t wither contentedly. It may be appropriate for Rachel to re-evaluate the responsibilities she’s carrying. She has been pouring herself into caring for her mother, leading church ministries, and working full-time. She should consider whether it would be wise for her to change her level of commitment, either temporarily or permanently. She might speak with her church leaders about delegating some responsibilities to others. She could look at whether other family members could help sometimes with caring for her mother.

Perhaps Rachel could do more to look after her own health and rest. It’s easy for her to think that serving others means neglecting her own needs, but physical rest and self-care are essential for long-term flourishing. She could practise a regular time of Sabbath rest each week. She might benefit from simple things like regular exercise, and making time for things that bring her joy. Perhaps Rachel might also find more support from her community. She might invite members of her church to help with meals, running errands, or even spending time with her mother to give her some respite. This is not a sign of weakness but a way to allow others to serve her in love. Rachel might also need to establish clearer boundaries for her teaching work, to prevent burnout. She could create specific times when she is ’off duty’ from work-related tasks, like grading papers or answering emails. By protecting her evenings or weekends, she can safeguard time to rest and connect with her family.

It is great that Rachel has learned to be content. If she can also learn to flourish, she will be able to serve God faithfully over the long-term.

Case Study 6 - Ruth (mid-20s)

Ruth has been a Christian since primary school, growing up in a family that valued faith and attended church regularly. As an adult, she’s actively involved in her church’s worship team, often leading others in praise and worship. To those around her, Ruth seems to be thriving spiritually and musically - she has a beautiful voice, and people frequently compliment her for how she helps lead the congregation into meaningful worship. But what others don’t see is the deep sense of insecurity that Ruth carries with her.

Despite her outward confidence, she constantly feels like she’s not good enough, whether it’s in her job, her friendships, or even her relationship with God. Even though people praise her for her musical talents, she often downplays their compliments, feeling like she doesn’t really deserve them. She tells herself that if they knew the real her - the one who doubts her abilities and struggles to trust God fully - they wouldn’t be so impressed.

Ruth also tends to compare herself with others, especially when it comes to her appearance and achievements. Social media is a big trigger for her. As she scrolls through her feeds, she sees friends and acquaintances posting pictures of their accomplishments, holidays, and seemingly perfect relationships. She finds herself wishing she were prettier, more successful, or more talented. In these moments, her insecurity takes over, and she starts to believe that she’ll never measure up.

Yet as well, Ruth often feels overwhelmed by the desire to prove her worth to others, becoming eaten up by the need for validation. She’s caught between feeling unworthy and trying to find her worth through accomplishments and the approval of others.

Recently, during a prayer time, Ruth broke down and shared with a close friend how much she struggles with insecurity. She feels guilty for even thinking about her own worth and worries that loving herself might be selfish or prideful. Yet, she also feels empty and exhausted from constantly seeking approval and never feeling at peace with herself.

elements.text:
Case Study 6b - Ruth indwelt by God’s truth

Ruth’s current struggle is a classic example of disordered self-love. Disordered self-love is not just about pride; it can also show up as anxiety and the need for constant validation. Ruth’s pattern of seeking approval from others will never satisfy her because our value is not based on human standards. True worth is rooted in God’s love for us and His creation of us as His beloved children.

To move forward, Ruth needs to see herself the way God sees her. That will help her embrace a rightly ordered, humble self-love.

Humble self-love knows that we are fallen, yet redeemed. Ruth needs to let this truth take up residence within her. She needs help in learning to shift her focus away from external comparisons and toward God’s truth about who she is. That way, she can rest in the knowledge that God already loves her fully and unconditionally, instead of seeking validation from others. Then she can escape the exhausting cycle of trying to prove her worth.

There are practical steps Ruth can take to help herself grow in this. She can take time to meditate on Scriptures that speak of her identity in Christ, so that these truths start to indwell and shape her. Replacing the lies of insecurity with God’s truth is a critical step in renewing her mind. She would be wise to limit her time on social media, since it sends her back into comparing herself to others. She may need to re-educate her inner voice, so that she speaks kindly and truthfully to herself, the way she would speak to others. She could also find help by sharing her struggles with trusted friends or mentors in her church community. They can offer her encouragement and remind her of God’s love when she’s feeling low.

As the truth of her worth in Christ begins to shape Ruth’s heart and mind, she will be better equipped to love others without seeking validation from them. Instead of relying on others to affirm her, she can serve in security and strength, knowing that her worth is already established in God. This frees her to love more selflessly, without the need to impress or compete.

Ruth will find true peace as she learns to rest in the knowledge that God delights in her. Self-rejection contradicts God’s own Word, that calls us ’Beloved.’ This is the foundation of a humble, rightly ordered self-love that leads to flourishing.

Case Study 7 - John (early-30s)

John came to faith at 27. He is married 8 years, has 2 kids and joined his church 6 years ago. Recently he started a new job with a probationary period, but 6 months in anxiety hits. He isn’t sleeping or eating well; he doesn’t know why he’s anxious.

John is heavily involved in church, leading Sunday School, serving as a deacon. He is keen to learn and has been to many church seminar days. He prays and reads his Bible often, ‘maybe not daily, but I certainly attempt to.’ He notices where help is needed, even when others don’t, and he will get stuff done; he is a hard worker. His marriage is strong, even compared with mature Christian couples.

John is a chronic nail biter. John remembers having stopped for nearly 4 months, but then he had a job interview he really wanted, and the stress started everything again. He hasn’t stopped since. John recalls a recent meeting with the eldership at church, where he was misunderstood, and seen as arrogant. It was a conversation about him becoming an elder. Before the meeting a friend who is an elder had suggested the outcome would be negative. John remembers going into the meeting feeling that there was no point in going ahead if the decision was already made.

John has a problem with porn. It was a struggle when he was first saved and it got better, although it still causes temptations, especially at more stressful times in life: deadlines in work, or maybe a bible study to prepare. He also talks about shouting at his children, finding parenting hard at times. He is constantly asking them to do the same things. His temper boils over a little too much for his liking.

For John school was difficult, he had a tough time with bullies and just wanting to fit in. He quickly went from girlfriend to girlfriend, rarely being outside of a relationship. At home John recalls a difficult relationship with his mother, they never got along. He had a good relationship with his uncle, his mother’s brother. As a teenager he went to work most summers with him. He remembers his uncle once breaking his wrist and being told to take it easy. This was during the school Easter holidays. John went to help him for 2 weeks, he was around 15 years old. He felt good because on the trip home his mother said, ‘I was told you worked really hard, well done.’ One other memory was when doing homework, John struggled with English and his mother got angry. He was around 12 years old, and clearly remembers his mother asking why he wasn’t as smart as the neighbour’s children. When asked about himself, John never talks about his good qualities. He focuses on the bad.

The proud man lives in fear of failure, and his anxiety comes from trying to hold up a false image. The humble man knows his value comes from God and rests in His assurance.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer

Pride is not thinking too much of yourself; it’s thinking of yourself too much. Anxiety follows when we are obsessed with our own significance.
Tim Keller

Pride is often a mask for our deepest anxieties, a way to cover our fragile ego.
Andrew Murray

elements.text:
Case Study 7b - Tell John a better story

Adult John needs to retell the story of his childhood. He needs to watch Jesus tell 12-year-old John a story about their heavenly Father who makes everyone special and unique, with different gifts, yet each is precious. Jesus says to young John:

Childhood is amazing for having fun and learning. As kids play and work, they find out what they are good at, what gifts God has given them. One day they will use those skills to bless others. Sometimes children struggle with this. They think everyone else’s gifts are better and get sad, or they think their gifts are the best and get proud. But gifts are as equally amazing as they are different. Enjoy your gifts and the gifts of everyone around you. The gifts are there for you to develop and enjoy and use to bring blessing to this broken world. Never be afraid to try stuff and fail, or to explore your gifts and make mistakes. You are exploring the person that God has made you, and He is delighted to see you try and fail and try again.

Sometimes when people are not feeling good about themselves, they say mean things to others. When someone says mean things like that to you, I want you to remember: it says more about how they are struggling than about you. I want to tell you a secret. Your mum is hurting. Someone has said mean things to her and she has said even meaner things to herself. She is feeling like a failure. She is hurting. And she is about to come over here and she wants to help you explore your gifts, but she can’t. And when she can’t, she is going to say something that she doesn’t believe and she doesn’t mean. And it will hurt. And it is something that no child should hear from their mother. And when she says it, I want you to see past her words and see her pain. This is not about you, it’s about her struggles. I want you to take the forgiveness I have given you and I want you to forgive her. She loves you. And even more, I love you. And you don’t need to be good at homework or anything else to get my love, you already have it, just look at the Cross - nothing could take my love from you. Now let’s sit here and try some more homework and together, we are going to explore your gifts and praise your father in heaven.

Those memories aren’t going away for adult John. They might be buried but what they need is the healing balm of the Gospel. Yes, John is guilty of disordered self-love, idolatry and pride. He needs to repent of seeking ultimate acceptance in the wrong places, but what he also needs is the Saviour. This is not a ’one time conversation.’ John will need to return to those childhood narratives many times, with Jesus by his side, telling a better, more truthful and gracious story.

Case Study 8 - Frank (mid-30s)

Frank is a Christian but struggles with identity, motivation and endurance in the Christian life. Frank was raised in a Christian home to caring parents. They lived in the countryside but were not farmers. His father was an outgoing people-person, who grew up in the town, and his mother an introverted countrywoman. He was the youngest child and grew up with little day to day interaction with anyone outside his family. He was taught not to be showy or proud but to quietly get on with life and to work hard. He trusted in Christ at an early age and was keen to please God at primary school which was very small. In academic selection (at aged 11) Frank’s siblings did not perform as well as hoped. Frank did better than expected. This was awkward for his parents to handle and confusing for Frank who was glad he did well but began to internalise that success was a source of embarrassment. Frank opted, with his parent’s encouragement, to go to the same high school as his siblings rather than the local grammar school as it was thought that he wouldn’t cope there. Throughout the rest of his school life he found that doing well in school came relatively easily but success was always something to be kept quiet or to be embarrassed about, at home and in school. In high school he fell between two groups of students: those raised in the farming community and those raised in the town (mostly from quite an aggressively loyalist area). Frank’s family lived in the countryside but were not farmers and so he felt he could not relate to either group.

As well as this, he was not maintaining a clear Christian witness and so maintained a lingering guilt. He had a feeling of not being comfortable either in his own skin or with those around him. He became highly afraid of saying or doing the wrong thing socially. Towards the end of high school the gospel began working on his heart; he began to be freed from the fear of man and started to follow Christ more closely. He began to serve in his church and on summer teams. After university and entering the working world he began with great hope for achievement and growth in his own life and in his work. The reality was, however, much more difficult and slow. There were many setbacks. He became afraid of failure and grew happy to just coast and please the people around him. Ambition and adventure in life became viewed as a suspicious source of pride or as too dangerous in case he fails. He struggles with self-discipline and establishing routines in his life. He recognises his lack of assertiveness over both his own life and his career and yet struggles to gain control. This in turn leads to further frustration and resignation.

Anxiety is often a byproduct of pride, where we think we must handle everything ourselves. In God’s hands, we find rest from both.
A.W. Tozer

Pride can mask itself as anxiety. We worry because we think we have to be in control. But when we humble ourselves, we learn to trust God with what we cannot manage.
Max Lucado

Case Study 8b - Tell Frank a better story

Frank needs to retell that story of his childhood, to have Jesus take 11 year old Frank by the hand and celebrate his academic achievement, to explain to him that his parents are trying to protect him, he needs Jesus to explain to 11 year old Frank that God has given him a wonderful gift to be used and celebrated and that God is going to equip little Frank with skills that are going to be a blessing in this broken world, that God’s grace in saving him from sin is the same amazing grace that sends him out in the name of Christ, confident that he is going to be used by God (Ephesians 2:8-10).

30 year old Frank needs to watch Jesus take 11 year old Frank by the hand and explain what happened. Assuming that Frank’s parents were trying to teach humility (rather than trying to suppress his gifts), 30 year old Frank needs to watch Jesus talk to 11 year old Frank, to assure him that his gifts are special and that he has been given them to be used and make a difference in this world, he needs to watch as Jesus encourages 11 year old Frank to forgive his father, maybe not for wilfully trying to damage Frank but for missing the impact of his words.

30 year old Frank needs to watch Jesus as he talks to 11 year old Frank, as Jesus asks him about all he learnt in School and watch how Jesus smiles from ear to ear, celebrating the heavenly Father that gives every good gift (James 1), he needs to watch as Jesus draws Frank close to himself and as they sit in the boat together, older Frank needs to watch as Jesus embraces little Frank, as he silently unties the rope and gently pushes the boat away from the harbour, and says to him, ‘let’s do this together’.

As Frank’s affections are reordered, as he stops fearing that godly ambition equals pride and family rejection, as Jesus’ words start to bring healing to his self-understanding, then he may have the freedom to develop godly ambition and drive.

Case Study 9 - Edward & Mary (late-40s)

Edward has just initiated and completed a divorce. He had been married to Mary for 15 years and they have 2 children together. Edward had lost interest in sex with Mary and when they went through the divorce, he told Mary that he had known for a long time that he didn’t feel like he loved her. He said he had always struggled with it and didn’t think he ever did really love her. He had tried to convince himself that he did, that’s why he married her, but he had been living a lie in their marriage.

A few months after the divorce, Edward calls Mary to say he has made a mistake. His life is empty, he needs her back.

  • Edward loves the healthy lifestyle. He has a strict exercise routine, only eats healthy food, treats his body like a temple. Sometimes obsessively so.
  • He only had one long term girlfriend before he married Mary. He broke up with her for the same reason. He didn’t feel like he really loved her.
  • He absolutely loves his job; he is a lawyer and he is passionate about what he does. He has been very successful and has a reputation for getting what he wants, even if he has to be ruthless with people to get it.
  • Apart from their wedding day, Mary has no memory of them spending any time with Edward’s parents. Occasionally Edward talks about his Dad and has fond memories. He never talks about his Mum. If Mary ever pushed for information, Edward would just say that she was a hard woman and they have drifted apart.
  • Edward’s mother was an insecure, angry lady. Edward craved to be hugged and cared for. At age 9 Edward came home after being seriously bullied and his mother showed no compassion and told him that he probably deserved it.

Take away all love and hatred, all hope and fear, all anger, zeal, and affectionate desire, and the world would be, in a great measure, motionless and dead.
Jonathan Edwards

elements.text:
Case Study 9b - Edward’s fears and desires

Despite what he said at the time, it seems Edward didn’t divorce Mary because of a lack of affection or desire for her, but because of his love for control, and his fear of emotional intimacy. Those desires and fears overshadowed his love for her (and his fear of loneliness). He believed that distancing himself from the relationship would solve his discomfort.

But once the divorce was final, Edward’s other fears - of isolation and loneliness - began to become dominant again, as did his love for Mary and their children. Without the relationship, his life felt empty, and he realised that Mary’s presence brought him a sense of stability and joy that he hadn’t fully appreciated. Edward’s call to Mary, months after the divorce, reveals a shift in the cycle of his desires. His need for control and distance is no longer in the driving seat, and he is becoming more and more conscious of his desire to reconcile and find meaning in the relationship he had discarded. He realises that his life feels incomplete without Mary and their children, and that the pursuit of his personal ambitions has left him unfulfilled.

However, unless Edward changes on a deeper level, he is likely to repeat the same cycle. Even if Mary took him back - or even if he eventually entered a relationship with someone else - unless he addresses the deep things going on in his heart, he will in time cycle back to his desire for control and fear of intimacy.

To move forward, Edward must confront the deep fears and desires that rule his life. He must learn to turn from them towards God as his foundation. His misshapen fears and desires flow from his disordered loves. He needs to understand that his desires can only be met in God, and his fears only overcome in God. Without correcting those foundations he will find it difficult to desire healthy relationships with others, and embrace vulnerability, rather than fear it. This will require repentance and a new understanding of how love works - not as a tool for control, but as a foundation of selfless connection, allowing his desires to be reshaped by God’s love and truth.

Case Study 10 - Glen and Jennifer (mid-30s)

Glen and Jennifer go to church. Jennifer comes across as a private person and doesn’t connect with many people at church. They don’t support the church financially and Jennifer hates always being asked to serve.

Glen’s Perspective: We’ve been married 5 years. I was attracted to Jennifer as she was so strong and driven and such a good mother to her son Bobby (he is 16). She says she doesn’t want any more children and won’t engage with the fact that I really do. It’s like she is always looking out for herself. She keeps her own savings account and even if things are tight, she’ll dip into it to go to a beauty salon, but I can’t touch it to help cover car repairs. She worked her way up to being the store manager at the local supermarket, but the rest of staff hate working for her. She micromanages them; everything has to be done her way. I know how they feel. Jennifer gets very jealous of me spending time with the lads. I used to go out with them on Fridays, but it caused arguments each time, so I stopped. Her son Bobby has started dating a lovely girl. Jennifer is nice to the girl’s face, but when she’s gone, Jennifer picks holes in her. I’ve told her that she can be selfish sometimes. She says she knows; her own mother used to say the same. She says she doesn’t want to be selfish and will try harder. I’ve told her that micromanaging people drives them away - she knew I was talking about more than the supermarket staff.

Jennifer’s Background: Her parents split when Jennifer was 11 years old, she was the oldest child of 4 siblings. Her father said he loved her very much and would still see her every weekend - but soon he just dissolved out of her life. Jennifer started secondary school aged 12. Her best friend from primary school was in her class. When her friend started to make new friends, Jennifer got so angry with her. It wasn’t long before they weren’t speaking. They never made up.

Her brothers and sisters were always quite ’care-free’, but Jennifer was an anxious teenager. She didn’t sleep well at night, and seemed on edge if her mum or siblings were gone for a long time. Her mother started to date another man, Jennifer made it clear that she didn’t want this man in the home even though she couldn’t point to anything wrong with him. Her mum told her off for not caring about anyone’s happiness but her own. As her siblings got older, Jennifer didn’t like sharing her stuff with them. Her mum and siblings said she was getting more and more selfish. Her mum would insist she shared, or take the stuff off her when she refused.

She worked hard at school and wanted a successful career. At university she started dating. Her boyfriend was charming, got her pregnant, and then left her. She raised her son Bobby alone and started working part time in the local supermarket. She taught him to ’work hard’ and ’tell the truth’. She often told him that people who lie are worthless. At 30 she married Glen. He’s a good husband and step-father.

Never be afraid to trust an unknown future to a known God.
Corrie ten Boom

elements.text:
Case Study 10b - Help Jennifer Feel Safe

Mistake: It is likely a mistake to rebuke Jennifer for selfishness, to call her to sacrificial giving, or to stop being ’me’ focused, to care for others.

Gospel Angle: Jennifer’s key problem is that she doesn’t feel safe, and so she cannot (or will not) entrust herself to others. The way she sees life, people take from her, and people leave. She needs to hear of the God who has pursued her, her whole life, and who sees her as precious. The Father who sees her brokenness, sin and shortcoming, and who loves her still! The Son who gave up everything to become human and die for her. The Good Shepherd who walks with her and will never leave her, who loved her so much he laid down his life for her to bring her forgiveness.

She seems selfish because she grips everything in a tight fist. We can rebuke her and tell her to open the fist; we can try to pull things out of her clenched fist; or we can show her she is safe. If we show her she is safe - and if she accepts that truth - then one day, her hand will open wide.

Think of how to gain the trust of an abused dog - you don’t scold it; you sit with it and share your food with it. You show it that you are safe.

For her Pastor: Jennifer’s situation cannot be rushed. Words are cheap to her - she has trusted people and their words in the past, and they let her down. She feels shame about her selfishness, so rather than rebuke her further, empathise and show that we all struggle. Praise her for how she has raised Bobby, and encourage her for the strength she has shown to get through her difficulties in life. Remind her that God walks with her. He knows our weakness - the bruised reed he will not break.

For her Church: Resist asking Jennifer to serve. To someone else, this would be a great way to bring them on board and help them feel like they belong. To Jennifer, it just feels like more people are trying to take from her. Find ways for folk in the church to serve her where it’s clear there are no ’strings attached’. If she is unwell, have someone drop round food.

For her friends & family - Glen: Glen should keep reassuring her that he loves her and is here to stay. He could treat her to the beauty salon with his money, praise her for the times she looks out for others, or tell her how much he appreciates it when she shows kindness to him or others.

For her friends & family - Bobby: Bobby should assure her that no-one could ever replace her as his Mum. His girlfriend is different, she is not a threat or a rival to Jennifer. He wants to one day be the husband for a lady that his dad never was to Jennifer - Jennifer has raised him that way.

Case Study 11 - George (mid-20’s)

George comes looking for help. He says his life is a mess and thinks that God is ashamed of him. He’s been addicted to porn since he was a teenager, and he’s been struggling with depression on and off for a few years.

George’s Background

  • George also thinks he might be gay - he is drawn to homosexual porn, particularly involving older men.
  • He also suffers from panic attacks.
  • George is an ’arts-y, sensitive’ young man. He was born into a rural farming family. All of his brothers are natural farmers. He is not.
  • His father loves him but is impatient with George, he doesn’t understand why George is so lacking in the skills his father values, and so weak emotionally. His father thinks he needs to toughen him up with ’tough-love’. Since George was a young boy, his father would shout at him if he made a mistake and tell him to pull himself together when George cried. Once when George was 7 and he got himself in a state because he left a gate open letting the cattle out onto the road, his father got so angry with his crying that he screamed at George to ’shut up and stop being pathetic!’
  • George can tell his father is proud of his farming sons, but not him.
  • George is still living at home, he has a part-time job but also helps out on the farm whenever he is needed. Since the age of 18, when George works with his dad, he gets anxious and his anxiety has turned into panic attacks.

We are not what we do. We are not what we have. We are not what other people think of us. We are the beloved daughters and sons of God.
Henri Nouwen

elements.text:
Case Study 11b - Help George know he’s valued

Mistake: In this situation, further ’tough love’ is unlikely to help George.

Gospel Angle: George needs to hear that he is special and unique, woven together in his mother’s womb. He needs to know that God loved him so much Christ died for him to forgive his sins. He needs to believe that God has seen George in his weakest most vulnerable state and yet God delights in him. There is no shame with God, he has cleansed us from our sins, we are clothed in Christ’s righteousness and beauty. God sees George exactly as he is - and God loves him. God has given each of us gifts. He has given George a unique set of gifts to bring blessing to those around him. He needs to know that ’ears aren’t blind.’ That’s the wrong way to look at people: ‘ears are designed to hear’. He needs to see that he has a purpose in this world, and to discover who God has designed him to be (and it’s not a farmer!), so that he can make a difference in this world to the glory of God.

For his Pastor: George needs someone to believe in him. Someone to help him explore who he is. His whole life, authority figures have told him he is a ’blind ear.’ There is a danger that, in the short term, an authority figure who shows George respect could be confusing for him, and sexual attraction could kick in. The pastor needs to avoid situations that could add to this interpretation, and also needs to not panic if there are signs of it.

For his Church: Give opportunities for George to explore and develop his gifts. Find an older man to mentor him, one who can encourage him and help him explore his gifts. In time teach George how he himself can become a mentor to younger men. In time, we want George to be able to see that he wasn’t pathetic as a boy, he just needed a compassionate authority figure to help him figure out who he was. Maybe George can be part of helping this be done for other young men, and maybe he can let Jesus do it for him.

That is worth trying for, but it is also worth knowing in advance that it might be a hard perspective for George’s father to embrace. Much the same is true for his brothers also. As to the issue of living at home - if there is no progress, George might need to be encouraged to take the next step of independence and move out. But some confidence building might need to happen first.

In terms of safety, value, and belonging, George needs help with all three: he needs to feel safe, he needs to feel he is valued, and he needs to belong. Most especially, perhaps, he needs to feel valued. It is also important that he comes to know safety, value and belonging both vertically (with God) and horizontally (with other people). He needs to base his primary sense of safety, value, and belonging on the vertical (God), but he also needs support with the horizontal (from his pastor, his church, and - ideally - his family and friends).

Case Study 12 - Stanley & Debbie (late-30s)

Stanley is a farmer, he has been married for 12 years and has three children. His wife, Debbie, is pursuing divorce, she began the process a couple of years ago but Stanley talked her out of it. She thought he might change but he hasn’t and she is set on leaving him. Debbie says that Stanley is married to the farm, he is never in the house, they don’t go on dates, they don’t go on holiday together, he doesn’t spend any time with the kids unless they are working with him. Stanley says he is doing his best to provide for his family and do an honest day’s work. He knows he should spend more time with his wife and kids and he desperately doesn’t want to lose them, but every time they have an argument about it, he makes an effort to be present in the home but it soon fades away. Debbie has had enough.

  • Stanley loves his father and looks up to him. When Stanley was 11, he was riding in the tractor with his Dad and on the road they got stuck behind traffic going to the local football match, some flashy BMW cars were in front of them and he saw his father get visibly agitated. His father said to Stanley: ‘Look at those wasters. They drive around enjoying themselves, spending their days watching football, probably living off the government, or their rich parents. It’s people like that that are destroying our country, they couldn’t do a day’s work if their life depended on it. They make me sick.’

elements.text:
Case Study 12b - Tell Stanley a better story

Aged 11, Stanley saw the look in his father’s eyes - the anger and disgust as he looked at those people. Stanley never wanted his father to look at him that way, and this fear shaped him. Unconsciously he began to fear that maybe he was a waster and that his dad would look at him with those eyes. He put his hope in hard work to win his dad’s respect. As a teenager he avoided TV, or going out with his mates. He worked late on the farm. He feared that if his dad ever really saw him, he’d see him as a waster, and look at him with those eyes. Hard work became his only hope. He spent the rest of his life running from that look. When he married and had kids, he loved them dearly, but he was still running. If he stopped to play with the kids, or take his wife out, his dad’s look would chase him. The farm was the only safe place. Stanley was hiding from himself, from everyone - scared that they would see him as a waster. Scared of those eyes. Yes, Stanley would look at Christ, but he was scared to let Christ look deep into his soul. To flourish, he needs to let Jesus in. He needs to watch Jesus take his 11-year-old self by the hand, as He speaks these words:

Your father loves you to bits. He has been through a lot and he is hurting. He has worked so hard his whole life and money has always been tight. He wanted to provide enough for his family, but when he couldn’t he began to hate himself, and in his pain, bitterness started to grow towards others who had an easy life. One day you saw that bitterness in his eyes, when he looked at those people in the fancy cars on the way to the football. That day you saw a look that left a scar on your soul. You feared that one day your dad would look at you that same way. But Stanley, I want you to see past the look and see your father’s pain. That look was not about you, it was about his struggles. In his pain, bitterness got a foothold, and that day it jumped from his eyes into your soul and you have been running ever since. That bitterness has put shadows in your soul and in your family. It has cost you peace in your soul, peace in your family, and it will cost you your farm. Your worth is not measured by how much you work. Your father loves you and your Heavenly Father loves you, I love you. I see your pain and I see your brokenness, I see the darkness in your soul that you are scared to look at, and I want to make this my home. I am here, in your heart to stay. I want you to see my eyes, as I look on you. I see the beauty within brokenness, you are loved, we are home, you don’t need to run any more.

When Stanley allows Jesus to gaze on him, he can stop running from his father’s eyes. He can spend time with the people he loves, enjoying the eyes of grace.

Case Study 13 - Andrew (mid-30s)

Andrew has been following Christ for the last five years. Before coming to faith, he lived a life that he’s not proud of. His past is filled with mistakes, including broken relationships, wasted opportunities, substance abuse, and decisions that hurt others. When Andrew accepted Christ, he experienced a massive sense of forgiveness and hope. For the first time in years, he felt free from his guilt and shame. He was baptised, and his church welcomed him warmly, reminding him that he is now a child of God.

However, as time has passed, Andrew has struggled to fully embrace his new identity. He finds himself haunted by memories of his past and feels that others, especially those who knew him before he became a Christian, still see him as the same old person. Although he is growing in his faith, reading the Bible, and attending church, Andrew sometimes feels like his old life is following him around. He wonders, ‘Am I really that different? Or am I just pretending to have changed?’

Andrew often feels discouraged, especially when he faces temptations or falls into old habits of thinking - or worse, when he relapses into old sins. (He is thankful this is becoming less frequent - but regularly depressed that he still falls into some of his old ways of behaving.)

He knows in his head that he has been born again, and is a child of God and a new creation in Christ - but his heart finds it difficult to believe that his past no longer defines him.

When Jesus rose again, God’s new creation emerged from the tomb, introducing a new way of being human, a new creation in which the broken pieces of the world are being put back together.
N.T. Wright

You are no longer what you used to be. You are a new creature in Christ. Your outward existence is the same, but your inner nature is marvellously changed.
Charles Spurgeon

elements.text:
Case Study 13b - Andrew (mid-30s)

Being made new in Christ is not a minor adjustment - it’s a total transformation. Anyone who is in Christ is a ’new creation.’ The old has gone, and the new has come. This means that Andrew is no longer defined by the mistakes he made in his past. Andrew needs to meditate on these truths until they dwell within him and begin to shape him. But this new life doesn’t happen automatically, without effort. For Andrew, this means recognising that his past mistakes no longer define him, but it also means actively working to let go of the habits, mindsets, and behaviours that belonged to his old life.

Andrew feels like his past is still following him around, but this is exactly why the Bible tells us to continually ’put off’ the old self and ’put on’ the new self. Every time Andrew resists temptations to fall into old patterns, he is living out his new identity in Christ. This doesn’t mean the old struggles will disappear instantly, but it does mean that Andrew has the power, through the Holy Spirit, to walk in newness of life.

Andrew needs to internalise the truth that God’s work in him is ongoing. He may still feel the weight of his past and the pull of old habits, but God is continually at work transforming him to be more like Christ. He can take comfort in knowing that being a new creation is not about never making mistakes - it’s about living in the assurance that God’s grace enables him to keep growing. God will never abandon him. He is faithfully working in Andrew’s life, even when progress feels slow.

Andrew can take steps to help himself fully embrace his new identity: Dwelling in the truth of God’s Word, especially the truth of his new identity in Christ, will help that truth dwell in him. Andrew might also benefit from connecting with a Christian mentor or accountability partner who can encourage him in his walk and remind him of his new identity when he’s feeling discouraged. Having someone to pray with and share struggles with can really help. Andrew needs to consciously surrender any lingering shame from his past to God. He can do this through prayer, asking God to help him release the weight of his old mistakes and to live in the freedom of being forgiven and made new. Each time Andrew chooses to live in a way that reflects his new identity - whether it’s showing kindness, resisting temptation, or making choices that honour God - he is ’putting on’ the new self. He can look for ways to actively practice living out this new creation, asking God for strength each day. His new life is a reflection of the resurrection power that raised Jesus from the dead.

Case Study 14 - Hannah (late 20s)

Hannah has been a believer for most of her life. She attends church regularly, listens to sermons, and volunteers for occasional events. But even though she has been involved for years, Hannah often feels like she doesn’t really belong in her church community. She’s friendly with people at church, but she hasn’t formed any deep relationships. Sometimes, she wonders if anyone would even notice if she stopped attending.

Recently, Hannah has been wrestling with a growing sense of isolation. While she enjoys her personal relationship with Christ, she has been noticing more and more that she doesn’t feel deeply connected to her church family. Every Sunday, she hears about being part of the body of Christ, but in practice, she feels like a distant spectator. When her pastor talks about community and serving one another, Hannah feels guilty for not being more involved, but she also feels unsure about how to take the next step. ’Isn’t it enough to just come to church and be a good Christian?’ she asks herself.

Hannah wants to experience the kind of deep, meaningful relationships she hears about in the Bible, but she isn’t sure how to make that happen.

The church is not a museum for saints, but a hospital for sinners. We are the living embodiment of the risen Christ in the world.
N.T. Wright

The body of Christ is a community of the redeemed, and our membership in it is by God’s grace. We live not as independent individuals but as members of one another.
Eugene Peterson

We need to recognize that we are not just members of a church; we are members of the body of Christ, and that identity shapes everything about our lives.

elements.text:
Case Study 14b - Hannah

Hannah needs to know that she already has a place in the body of Christ. The body of Christ is made up of many members, and each is vital to the whole. Hannah may feel like a spectator, but in reality, she is an indispensable part of Christ’s body, simply by virtue of her faith in Christ. Her feelings don’t change the truth that she belongs. Hannah’s life is intertwined with the lives of other believers. She is connected to the church in a deep, spiritual way, even when she doesn’t feel it.

There are different possible reasons why Hannah is struggling to connect. The problem might be (mostly) on her side. Perhaps she hasn’t fully embraced the idea that being part of the body of Christ means active participation, not just passive attendance. She could explore how her gifts can serve the body. Or it might be that she hasn’t taken the time (or doesn’t know how) to develop genuine, Christ-centred relationships where she and others can encourage and strengthen one another. Hannah could make progress by joining a small group or inviting a fellow church member for a meal. Building meaningful relationships takes time, but as Hannah invests in her church community, she will begin to see how those connections deepen her sense of belonging. As she shifts her focus to actively participating and serving, Hannah will likely experience the joy that comes from living out her calling as a member of Christ’s body. By serving others, she will begin to see how God uses her to bless the church and fulfil His mission in the world.

It is also worth acknowledging that the problems may be less (or, at least, not completely) on Hannah’s side. Some church communities are structured in a way that makes it hard for at least some people to integrate well. Perhaps the church community is not very good at integrating newcomers, or single people, or couples without children, or older people, or foreigners, or those from a different background to everyone else. Problems like this are not always easy to see, and nor are they quick to fix (and Hannah may not be in a position to fix them). It is never a good idea to jump to the conclusion that the problem in a situation lies wholly (or mostly) with someone else, and not with us, although it is worth Hannah being aware that in some circumstances a church community may not be structured in such a way that it can easily accommodate and integrate people like her. Being a member of the body of Christ is both a gift and a responsibility. It is a gift both to the individuals and the community, and a responsibility upon both the individuals and the community.

Case Study 15 - David (early 30s)

David is passionate about his faith and actively involved in his church. He attends Bible studies, volunteers regularly, and leads a small group. On Sundays, David feels close to God and is encouraged by his identity in Christ. But when Monday comes, and he returns to work, that sense of identity fades.

David works as a marketing manager for a large company. The working environment is competitive and high-pressure. His colleagues often use underhanded tactics to get ahead, and there is a strong emphasis on success and performance. David struggles to live out his faith. He finds himself cutting corners, exaggerating results, sometimes telling outright falsehoods, and going along with office gossip just to fit in and avoid conflict. By the end of the working week, David feels drained and guilty, knowing that he isn’t living as the person God has called him to be.

David wants to be the same person at work as he is at church, but he feels stuck. He wonders, ‘How can I live out who I am in Christ, in a place where success seems to come at the cost of integrity?’ He wonders if it is even possible to reflect Christ in his actions when everyone else is playing by different rules.

Living out who we are in Christ means letting our identity inform our actions. We are called to reflect His love in every aspect of our lives.
Tim Chester

The way we live reflects what we believe about God. If we truly understand our identity in Christ, it will overflow into our daily lives.
John Piper

You were made for a mission. When you live out your identity in Christ, you begin to fulfill the purpose for which you were created.
Rick Warren

elements.text:
Case Study 15b - David being who he is

David needs to be shaped by the truth that his identity in Christ is constant, no matter his environment. Whether he’s in church or at work, he is a new creation in Christ. His identity doesn’t change based on his surroundings. God calls us to be holy in all areas of life, reflecting His character wherever we go. David’s work environment may tempt him to compromise his values, but his identity in Christ means that he is called to something greater. He is a child of God in all situations.

David’s struggle to live out his identity in Christ at work is understandable - he faces real pressures. But God promises to be with us and strengthen us, even in difficult circumstances. David doesn’t have to face these challenges alone; he can rely on God’s strength to help him stand firm in his identity, even when it’s hard. David can begin to trust that God’s plan for his life includes integrity and faithfulness, even if it doesn’t seem to lead to immediate success by the world’s standards. By trusting God, David can choose to act with honesty and love, knowing that his ultimate reward comes from God, not from his boss or colleagues.

For David, this might mean making small but significant changes in how he interacts with his colleagues. Instead of going along with office gossip, he could choose to speak words that build others up. Instead of cutting corners to meet deadlines, he can commit to doing his work with integrity, trusting that God will honour his faithfulness. God has prepared good works for us to do, and that includes the work we do in our daily lives. David’s job is not just a means to an end - it’s part of his mission as a follower of Christ. By seeing his work as an opportunity to reflect Christ’s love, David can find renewed purpose.

Instead of viewing his workplace as a battleground where he has to compromise to survive, David can see it as a mission field where he is called to be the hands and feet of Jesus. David can shine the light of Christ in a place where it may not be readily visible. David is not responsible for how others respond to that light. Some may be drawn to find out more, others may be provoked to oppose the light. Some people may be intrigued by the difference in how he lives, others may respond with resistance, criticism or even open hostility. If David lives out who he is in Christ, it may help his career, or it may hinder it. He might get promoted because of his integrity, or he might get fired because of it. It is not David’s responsibility to control those outcomes. His responsibility is simple: to be who he is in Christ.

paras: BeaconLight is a non-denominational Christian training organisation based in the UK, founded in 1995. Its aim is to equip Christians worldwide with practically-applied Biblical gospel ministry tools — resources designed to help people both equip themselves and equip others.

BeaconLight’s resources include CrossCheck, which enables Christians to explain their faith and lead others to Jesus, and Word@Work, a verse-by-verse applied devotional commentary of the whole New Testament. BeaconLight also provides printed Biblical resources to prisons, seafarers, police, and the armed services.
BeaconLight believes that Christian ministry should be free of charge, and all its online materials are available without registration or payment. The ministry is funded entirely by donations.
